title: Integrating XState with React
description: Connect XState machines to React components using @xstate/react, including useMachine, useSelector, and testing strategies.

data.text: Welcome to this comprehensive guide on **Integrating XState with React**. Connect XState machines to React components using @xstate/react, including useMachine, useSelector, and testing strategies. In today's rapidly evolving technology landscape, understanding this topic is crucial for any developer looking to build robust, scalable, and maintainable applications. This lesson will take you from fundamental concepts to advanced implementations, providing you with practical knowledge you can apply immediately. Whether you are a beginner taking your first steps or an experienced developer looking to deepen your expertise, this guide has something valuable for you. We will explore theoretical foundations, practical implementations, real-world scenarios, and common pitfalls to avoid. By the end of this lesson, you will have a thorough understanding of Integrating XState with React and be confident in applying it to your projects.

blocks.text: XState is framework-agnostic by design, but it ships with first-class React bindings in the @xstate/react package. These bindings handle subscribing to actor state changes, re-rendering components only when relevant state slices change, and cleaning up listeners on unmount. The two primary hooks are useMachine for simple cases and useSelector when you need to select specific pieces of state from a larger machine.

blocks.title: Actor Model in XState v5
blocks.text: XState v5 uses the actor model terminology. A machine becomes an actor when you pass it to createActor. The useMachine hook is syntactic sugar that creates, starts, and stops an actor for you.

blocks.caption: Data flow from an XState actor into a React component.
blocks.definition:
flowchart LR
    Machine[XState Machine] --> Actor[createActor]
    Actor --> Service[Running Service]
    Service --> |state changes| Hook[useMachine / useSelector]
    Hook --> |derived state| Component[React Component]
    Component --> |send event| Actor

blocks.text: useMachine is the simplest way to connect a machine to a React component. It returns a tuple containing the current actor snapshot and a send function. When the machine transitions, the component re-renders with the new snapshot. The send function accepts event objects or strings, matching the event types declared in your machine configuration.

blocks.title: useMachine with a Fetch Machine
blocks.content: A practical example connecting a data-fetching machine to a React component.

blocks.text: Prefer state.matches('stateName') over string equality on state.value. matches() is type-safe and works correctly with nested and parallel states.

When a machine is large, you do not want your component to re-render on every state change. useMachine always returns the full snapshot, but you can derive only the data you need using useSelector. The selector function receives the full snapshot and returns a value. React will only re-render when that selected value changes by reference, just like Redux selectors.

blocks.title: useSelector for Granular Updates
blocks.content: Subscribe only to the data you need to avoid unnecessary renders.

blocks.title: When to Use useMachine vs useSelector
items: useMachine: the component renders different UI for every state (loading, error, success).
useSelector: the machine is large, and the component only cares about a small slice of state or context.
useMachine: simpler mental model for small to medium machines.
useSelector: better performance characteristics for high-frequency state updates.

blocks.text: Because XState machines are pure logic, the best tests run against the machine itself, not the React wrapper. Use XState's built-in test utilities to simulate event sequences and assert on the final state and context. React component tests can verify that the correct UI renders for each machine state using testing-library queries.

blocks.title: Testing a Machine Without React
blocks.content: Unit test the machine logic directly with XState's test utilities.

blocks.text: Never test statechart logic inside React component tests alone. If the machine logic is buggy, the component test will still pass because it only verifies the UI. Unit-test the machine first, then write thin component tests to verify rendering.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
points: useMachine is the simplest hook for connecting an XState actor to a React component.
useMachine returns the full snapshot and a send function on every render.
useSelector subscribes to derived slices of actor state to minimize unnecessary re-renders.
Prefer state.matches() over checking state.value directly for type-safe state checks.
Test machines in isolation first using createActor and send, then verify UI rendering separately.

data.text: Common Mistakes to Avoid

Even experienced developers can fall into these traps when working with **Integrating XState with React**. Being aware of these common mistakes will help you write better code and avoid costly debugging sessions:

items: **Over-Engineering**: Using advanced features of Integrating XState with React when a simple solution suffices. Always start with the simplest approach that meets your requirements and add complexity only when justified.
**Ignoring Edge Cases**: Failing to handle null values, empty states, and boundary conditions leads to runtime errors and poor user experience.
**Copy-Paste Without Understanding**: Using code snippets without fully understanding their implications creates hidden bugs and security vulnerabilities.
**Neglecting Testing**: Assuming code works without tests is a recipe for production incidents. Write tests that verify behavior and prevent regressions.
**Performance Blindness**: Ignoring performance implications until they become critical issues. Profile early and optimize based on data, not assumptions.
**Hardcoding Configuration**: Embedding values directly in code instead of using environment variables and configuration files.
**Tight Coupling**: Creating dependencies that make code difficult to test, modify, or reuse. Favor composition over inheritance.
**Inconsistent Error Handling**: Mixing different error handling patterns makes code unpredictable and hard to debug.

data.text: Performance Considerations

Performance is a critical aspect of any production application. When implementing **Integrating XState with React**, consider these optimization strategies to ensure your application remains fast and responsive:

items: **Lazy Loading**: Defer non-critical operations until they are actually needed to reduce initial load time.
**Caching**: Implement intelligent caching strategies to avoid redundant computations and network requests.
**Memoization**: Cache results of expensive function calls to improve performance for repeated operations.
**Batch Processing**: Group multiple operations together to reduce overhead and improve throughput.
**Resource Management**: Properly clean up resources, event listeners, and subscriptions to prevent memory leaks.
**Profiling**: Use performance profiling tools to identify bottlenecks before optimizing.
**Bundle Size**: Minimize dependencies and use tree-shaking to reduce application bundle size.
**Network Optimization**: Reduce payload sizes, use compression, and implement efficient data fetching strategies.

data.text: Security Considerations
Security should never be an afterthought. When implementing **Integrating XState with React**, keep these security best practices in mind to protect your application and users:

items: **Input Validation**: Always validate and sanitize user input to prevent injection attacks.
**Authentication and Authorization**: Implement proper access controls and verify user permissions.
**Secrets Management**: Never hardcode API keys, passwords, or tokens. Use environment variables and secret management services.
**HTTPS**: Always use HTTPS in production to encrypt data in transit.
**Content Security Policy**: Implement CSP headers to mitigate XSS attacks.
**Dependency Scanning**: Regularly scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities.
**Rate Limiting**: Protect APIs from abuse with appropriate rate limiting.
**Audit Logging**: Log security-relevant events for monitoring and incident response.
